patterns: is cardio the same as aerobic
how often should i do cardio
entries.answer: Cardio is any exercise that raises heart rate for a sustained period, and it is the category most people mean when they say they need to get fit. The measure that matters is not the heart rate at its peak but how much of the week is spent in a range where talking becomes difficult. That range is the one that changes fitness, and it is lower than most beginners assume, which is why easy sessions do more than they appear to.

entries.answer: Progressive overload is the principle that a muscle adapts only when it is asked to do more than it currently can, and it applies to almost every kind of training rather than just weightlifting. The extra can be weight, repetitions, distance, or difficulty, and it has to be small and gradual. Doing too much too fast is what produces injury rather than progress, since tendons and connective tissue adapt more slowly than muscle does.

entries.answer: Mobility is the range a joint can move through, and it is separate from flexibility, which is the length of a muscle at rest. Strengthening a range that a joint cannot actually use is the usual mistake, since a heavy squat through a restricted ankle does not train the squat, it trains compensation. The practical work is moving each joint through its full range unloaded and slowly, which most people find uncomfortable and therefore skip, and that discomfort is the useful signal.

entries.answer: Deload is a week of reduced training volume, and it is the least popular part of a programme because it feels like going backwards while the training log still looks empty. The reason it works is that fitness and fatigue are separate: a hard week builds both, and the fitness outlasts the fatigue while the fatigue does not. Cutting the volume for a week while keeping the intensity lets the fatigue clear without losing the adaptation.

entries.answer: A warm-up raises temperature and primes the movement pattern before the main effort, and it is not the same as stretching, which is a separate and much more debated activity. What actually helps is moving through the specific actions about to be performed, lightly at first, so the nervous system has run the pattern once. Static stretching held for a long time before a sprint can temporarily reduce force output, which is why the long holds are discouraged immediately before competition.

patterns: how much water should i drink
entries.answer: Hydration is the balance between the fluid a body takes in and the fluid it loses, and in hot weather or during exercise the losing side wins by default because sweat is the body's main cooling mechanism. Sweat cools by evaporating, which is why a humid day is harder on you than a dry one at the same temperature: the sweat cannot evaporate fast enough, so you sweat more and cool less. The signs of losing too much are thirst, a dark colour in the urine, headache, dizziness and tiredness, and the order matters because thirst arrives late relative to the actual loss. During exercise the practical advice is to drink ahead rather than to wait, to take in fluid every fifteen or twenty minutes, and to add salt when the session is long or the sweat is heavy, since a very long run can strip salt as well as water. The overcorrection is also real and less well known: drinking a very large amount of water in a short time can itself cause a dangerous condition, so a person should drink according to loss rather than to a rule about how much water is healthy.

entries.answer: Endurance is the capacity to keep an effort going over time, and it is a quality rather than a single number: it depends on how long, how hard, and at what intensity, which is why someone can have enormous endurance in one sport and none in another. Physically it rests on the aerobic system, which supplies energy using oxygen, and the limit is how fast the heart and lungs can deliver oxygen to the working muscle rather than how much oxygen is present, which is why training at altitude is a real technique. It is also limited by the muscles' own ability to clear lactate, since a sprint depends on energy made without oxygen and clearing the by-product of that is what allows a second effort. Training builds it through a larger and denser network of blood vessels, so the same effort moves less blood and costs less, and the gain is slow and specific to the kind of work done. The practical test is that an endurance base is built with long efforts, not with sprints, and a schedule that is only hard ends up producing a person who is quick and cannot finish.
